>since you could just rotate cards within each category a discipline
>has an acess to.

Creates other problems, such as annoying lots of folks.



Getting back to a central point, while a lot of people really dislike the idea
that they can no longer play cards when a game rotates them out, it's not
really any different in a competitive environment from new cards making old
ones obsolete.

>So what do you suggest ? Banning 100 most abusive cards in the game ?
>Guess what ? Even after that another 100 most abusive cards appear.

Ideally, you deal with those cards that have effectively banned a significantly
larger number of cards. Banning a few cards to make 50 cards playable may well
be constructive where making 10 playable wouldn't be.

>The number of cards played in given format is some percentage of
>number of cards in format. The greater the number of cards in format ,
>the smaller the percentage.

Generally true, but if cards were, across the board, more specialized, it
wouldn't necessarily have to be.

Note, at the same time, suddenly making cards highly specialized without making
sure they are worth playing in tournament level decks is just printing a bunch
of coasters.

>So grouping library cards would actually make more of your cards
>playable in the
>long run. I can't see why it is bad thing.

>> > Grouping of vampires basically creates kind of 'block constructed'

>> > crypt but the catch is that no crypt 'cycle' phase out entirely (you
>> > can STILL play with group 1 vampires). It also enables to print new
>> > and interesting vampires which do have an impact (and think about how
>> > many of new CE vampires would not have an impact if grouping rule
>> > didn't existed)
>>
>> But you could just print those cards without grouping. As I reject
>> your reasoning WRT using Magic as an example which explains why grouping
>> vampires is necessary, I likewise reject the necessity of grouping
>> vampires altogether. Curt Adams may document certain somewhat
>> significant effects of dial-a-crypt over the course of one base set to
>> two base sets plus several expansions of varying sizes. That's to be
>> expected since we're starting from a very small pool to one several
>> times its size. But I think it's reasonable to expect that factor to
>> level off over time. Grouping is really unnecessary to allow newer
>> players to compete.
>
>Magic and VTES have MANY things in common. Almost any given Magic
>concept have
>VTES equivalent and vice versa.

And, so it is with most CCGs.

>I would rather identify a possible problem , analyze it and prevent
>it. The let us destroy a world so we can built it anew attitude is
>something I do not subscribe to.

It is possible, however, that the cure is worse than the ill. A lot of CCGs
don't last long enough for the problem of bloat to matter. So, resetting the
playing field hasn't been done that often, nevermind that CCGs are less than 10
years old. This game has had the "advantage" of having numerous redundant
effects which has effectively reduced the number of real strategies which has
helped keep it under control (with a cost in variety).

The important thing is how often will the game see expansion v. the rate at
which expansion is escalating the power level. The higher either is, the more
important the problem. Neither seems that high relative to what they could be.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Iain Wilson wrote:
> Yes, it's inconvenient that some cards "don't do what they say on the
> tin" but most players either know the erratas, or else (if they're
> newbies) they're playing with the newly printed versions of the cards
> anyway...

But the issue become more pernicious the more cards get errata. The
fact that errata needed to be used to deal with the overpowered cards
seems to be leading to a complete lack of sensitivity to the drawback
of changing cards. It's a minor drawback but it adds up.

If you don't think so, then why even print *any* text on a card? In
the future, White Wolf should just issue cards with serial numbers and
no text at all on them - at the various rarity levels by the usual
number of these things and all that: say 1 rare, 3 uncommon, 2 vampires,
and 5 commons per pack. Then, on release day, they can update "The
Book". "The Book" has all the current card text so we can walk around
with decks of cards that just have serial numbers on them and "The Book"
will tell us what the cards mean. If any cards need to be errataed in
the future, White Wolf need only modify "The Book" electronically and
stamp a new date on it and then announce (via newsgroup, mail lists, and
such) that a new book exists. We can all download it and print it or
carry it around on notepad computers and look up the new versions as
we need them.

If this doesn't sound like such a hot idea to you, then you need to
admit that at some point the concept that any card can be modified
at any time for any reason, no matter how trivial, is going too far.

> If you don't like it, you don't have to play with the "new cards".

GOSH, it sure would be nice if that were true! But of course, it's not.
To be fully competitive in a competitive game, I need to make use of all
viable tools offered or I'm crippling myself. But never mind that, even.
Even if never use a modified card, the fact is that my opponents can and
I have no control of what they put in their deck. In fact, these kinds
of things are worse in an opponent's deck. At least he had the chance
to look up his cards before he built them into the deck. I have to be
aware there's even a change before I can think to look it up - as I'm not
going to constantly look up every card all my opponents use as they use
them because that would be insane.

Fred

Messages.Author: Jozxyqk
Messages.Body:
> If you don't think so, then why even print *any* text on a card? In
> the future, White Wolf should just issue cards with serial numbers and

You know what?
As silly and bitter as the intent of this post is, I kinda like that idea
for a card game.
The cards have pretty art, a name, and a bar code.. and you get a
book, or a barcode scanner, or a computer program, that tells you what the

I'm not saying do it for V:tES, but it's a neat idea, in theory, for

Heroclix mini over a scanner and see what his current abilities are...

It's not vast enough. Last I looked, T1.5 still allowed things liked
Juzam Djinn, Ernam Djinn, and other things that they'd never print nowadays.
The fact that they _wouldn't_ print such a thing in a current expansion tells
you there's a problem. And that is my exact point.

(from further down she wrote)

> Grinning Demon is comparable to Juzam

Haven't seen it but I would be shocked. "It's the 'new' Juzam!" has been old joke
on the Magic newsgroup for years. They've had a million years to print something
comparable to Juzam Djinn and they've never done it and I doubt they've done it
recently. Unless they shot their entire design group in the last two years and
replaced them with evil changelings. In any case, such a change in policy would
be a recent event and you therefore couldn't use the previous experience you'd
had with T1.5 to say anything about Jyhad. You'd have to wait some number of
years for them to continue printing a lot of new cards that were as good as the
still-allowed oldest good cards in T1.5

Extended still allowed multilands last I looked. They stopped printing multilands
and proceeded to design cards after 4th edition as if multilands didn't exist. At
some point, extended will lop of all the base sets and expansions that included
anything really bad and will likely become a fairly balanced game that point.
(They may have already done it. I haven't look lately.) That's only because all
of the real problem cards were in the oldest expansions. Even now, however, if
they print an overpowered that's not absolutely gamebreaking, they don't bother to
errata it or ban it or anything. They just let it sit there and fester, causing
a number of other cards to be much less useful because they don't measure up to a
game filled with top-of-the-heap power cards. In V:tES, that's not true, so I
would absolutely expect our experience in this sense to differ.

This point to me is just not debatable. If you want to believe T1.5 is balanced,
go ahead. If nothing else, simply the amount of time it

> Hovewer almost no-brainer cards do exists in V:TES , one classic
> example would be a blood doll (and I am not saying it is broken, I am just saying
> that most people when they create decks put 3-5 copies of blood doll
> automatically in)

I build lots of decks without Blood Dolls. Some people may say that's why I don't
win as often as I could and perhaps that's true. But there are certain types of
decks that simply don't need them.

In any event, what you're talking about is not an overpowered card. It's called
a "staple", and it differs from overpowered cards in that its function is
consciously intended by the designers. In theory, they could issue other cards
that fill similar functions but frequently, the one card fills the function so
well that they just make it a common and assume people will use them in large
numbers. In the case of Blood Dolls, there's Tribute to the Master, which can
work better in a weeny deck and Minion Tap which can work better in a high-cap
vampire deck, and things like Consanguineous Boon if you want to trust your
ability to call and pass votes, but Blood Doll is probably the best one. And
that's fine. You just reprint it on a regular basis and everyone, old and new,
can use it.

> And besides in such formats you have probably 10 000 + cards to choose
> from, with ANY power curve in such format most cards would not be played.
>
> Contrary to popular belief here, VTES DO have a power curve. Sure, not such
> a steep one as say Morphing vs Air Elemental but there still is here.
> Why would then almost everyone play with Govern and not so many
> peoples play with Scouting Mission ? (and before anyone gives me
> examples of decks where SM is better that GtU , yes I know that they
> exists, there are but few compared to decks where GtU is better)

It's impossible for there _not_ to be a power curve. There's no way to make
all cards exactly equal in power. There is a difference, however, in the
designer philosophy for Magic cards and the designer philosophy for V:tES
cards (since LSJ took control, at least) as I noted in my previous post.
That difference is why having 10,000+ V:tES cards to choose from will not
cause the same problem as having 10,000+ Magic cards to choose from. And
Magic could be fixed, too, if the DCI had a desire to do so.

> > Also, the Magic designers don't seem to hold themselves to a very high
> > standard in terms of balance in general. So even in a single set even in
> > recent years, there's still far much variation in the value of various
> > cards.
>
> I do believe that Magic is far more balanced than it was say two or
> three years before (by Magic I mean extended, T2, block constructed)

I agree. They definitely got distinctly better over time. But they've
never gotten to the point of being totally honest (either with themselves or
with the public, I'm not sure which) about the overpowered old cards and what
truly needs to be done about them. Or about "somewhat overpowered" new cards,
for that matter.

> Do you consider banning of the card (RtI) a way of fixing it ? :)

Yes, I do. (Who was the American General who said of South Vietnam, "We
had to destroy these people to save them."?) It "fixes it" in the sense
that RtI is not dominating the game preventing people from using other cards
because RtI is too good to ignore. (And using the various support cards for
RtI and the cards that best defend against other players' RtI cards, etc.)

> In other post you stated that ToR3 was wallpaperized, now you use it
> as an example of pointing differences between Magic and V:TES :)

I'm not sure what you fail to understand. An overpowered card causes people
to ignore the large, "middle" class of cards because they want to use the
best cards they can use. A wallpaper card only causes people to ignore one
single card: the wallpaper card. The problems of overpowered cards and
wallpaper cards are not equivalent problems. The former is clearly much
more destructive to deckbuilding games.

> Would you thing that some of the following things would be good for
> the game:
>
> 1)printing 5 more aus/AUS intercept cards
> 2)printing 5 more obf/OBF stealth cards
> 3)printing 5 more for/FOR prevent cards
> 4)printing some more ANI intercept cards
> 5)printing some more free OBT stealth cards
> 6)printing more dominate bleed cards
> 7)printing more presence bleed cards
>
> 1) would lead to players putting 4-6 enhanced senses in the deck
> and rest intercept slots would be filled with single copies of given
> intercept cards avaiable, that way one entire principle of

> game/deckbuilding would be, well nonexistant.

>
> 2) same as 1 with regard to stealth

I assume you refer to the rule about playing identical action modifier
and reaction cards on the same action. My opinion is simply that there
are already so many different types of these cards that it really doesn't
come up much if players want to avoid the problem anyway. So it doesn't
strike as changing the game much to give them yet more options. Often,
however, they want one particular function such as the maneuver granted
by Spirit's Touch at superior. If so, then they wind up needing to use
multiple copies of Spirit's Touch instead of just any old intercept
reaction card and the rule will come into play. If they were to start
printing cards that had exactly the same function with different names,
then it would change the game over time.

> 3),6),7) - the cards would be too good or too bad compared to what we
> have in their categories now. Both options are not good.

It isn't clear to me that such cards would necessarily be too good or
too bad. I agree it's bad if it happens. But if such cards are too
bad, you've wasted some cardboard. If they're too good, then that's
when errata things.

>
> 4),5) - the entire balance between disciplines would be throwed out of
> window in process

It could be. You can simply reprint the existing free OBT stealth cards
or ANI intercept cards in future expansions if it's the designers' intent
to limit the number of different named cards. So this is not really an
issue, either.

> You could argue that no such cards need to be printed. Hovewer how can
> you print many new cards for many of current disciplines that would be in
> flavour of given discipline?

Given my individual responses to the various situations you listed above,
I don't believe this is an issue.

> > Over time, continuing to add more and more new cards should not cause

> > > -because many cards otherwise not playable in other constructed
> > > formats are playable here (or biggest percentage of cards you buy are
> > > actually playable besides in draft)
> >
> > All this amounts to is basically banning cards by card set that should
> > be banned or errated on an individual basis. You really can't draw any
> > conclusions from the experience of Magic. When unbalanced card problems
> > are actually dealt with correctly, I think you discover that *more* cards
> > get used and are considered playable over the course of printing more
> > cards. Not less.
>
> So what do you suggest ? Banning 100 most abusive cards in the game ?
> Guess what ? Even after that another 100 most abusive cards appear.

That's the old Magic newsgroup refrain, isn't it? My reply to it is invariable:
cards that are randomly distributed in terms of what can loosely be called,
"power". This distribution is a classic bell-shaped curve in which the most
powerful cards are a relative few located at the top of the curve. Lop off
this thin "tip" of the curve and other cards will, indeed become "the most
powerful". However, once you've lopped off enough of the tip, the cards left
on top are only a little bit more powerful than most of the rest of the cards
in the middle. At that point, the game is now much better because it's much
harder to choose the best cards and strategies. Life is now good.

Rather than banning cards, of course, you can errata them. WotC goes to the
other side of errata fanaticism: they almost entirely refuse to do it at all,
ever. That's their choice but regardless of which choice they make, it's much
better than simply ignoring the problem which they've done. And yes, in T1.5,
a *lot* of cards would need to be dealt with. Dozens, maybe over a hundred,
just because they printed so many cards before the idea of game balance
penetrated the thick skulls of the Magic design team. That's unfortunate, but
it still doesn't help to ignore a real problem that exists and pretend T1.5
is balanced in its current form. It isn't. Not even close.

> The number of cards played in given format is some percentage of
> number of cards in format. The greater the number of cards in format ,
> the smaller the percentage.

I disagree.

> So grouping library cards would actually make more of your cards
> playable in the long run. I can't see why it is bad thing.

It's a bad thing because 1) it's not necessary, 2) it's too complicated, and
3) it clearly annoys people.

> > > The extended format (where you can use cards from last 3-4 such
> > > cycles) is also very popular (although sometimes not very balanced)
> > >
> > > The problem is that even in extended cards phase out in T1 void.
> > > (because it becomes impossible to balance it)
> >
> > (Sigh) It's not impossible to balance it. The DCI simply refuses to
> > do so.
>
> Worldgorger Dragon/Animate Dead combo is clear example that it is
> impossible to balance vast formats while still printing new cards.
> Note that both cards are O.K. on their own. The only problem is that they
> exist simultaneously in given format.

I think it's somewhat tricky to do at times. Particularly in Magic, where
combinations of cards has a different meaning than Jyhad. In Magic, the
4-card limit is now an accepted part of the game. (Original, Richard
Garfield claimed it was not. For a while, there was talk of designing it
out. Eventually, they just gave up and accepted it.) Between the 4-card
limit and the 60-card deck minimum, card combinations are in most cases
somewhat difficult to pull off. (Note how the various "Tutor" cards
drastically modify the chance of pulling off card combo, ultimately
causing them to get banned in T1.5 as the designers finally realized how
tricky they were to design around.) Because card combos are a low odds
proposition, they must have a high payoff when two cards with synergy
appear together or no one would ever use them at all. The trouble is that
designing combo cards that do something worthwhile enough to have that
high payoff can be very risky when there are so many other cards out there
that a designer and all the playtesters can't remember and try out all the
possibilities.

Dealing with such things is really not so hard but the DCI handcuffs
themselves by refusing to consider timely bannings or the use of errata.
There's a mentality in the DCI that insists on just living with all their
mistakes unless a mistake is of certain magnitude. Also, V:tES does not
have the same problem because all V:tES cards are designed to be used in
combinations in the first place. V:tES has no card limits so the designers
are much more mindful of the sorts of things they must never do. For instance,
I notice they avoid designing cards that make burning a vampire during minion
phase easy, as this combos powerfully with things like Mind Rape and Spirit
Minionette. Likewise, they avoid designing cards that steal another player's
vampire over the course of Untap and Master phases, when it could be
sacrificed to things like Golconda and Khobar Towers. It's tricky stuff, but
the designers are used to avoiding pitfalls.

> Magic and VTES have MANY things in common. Almost any given Magic
> concept have VTES equivalent and vice versa.

They may have things in common, but they also have many serious
differences. In determining whether to use experience from Magic to
decide what to do about V:tES, the differences are far more important
than the similarities.

> > > Grouping of library cards would open vast posibilities for new cards
> > > and abilities which do have an impact and are not broken (and it may
> > > become a problem otherwise in (not so) distant future)
> >
> > It is unlikely to become a problem. At least, let it become a true
> > problem and then we can evaluate what to do about it. The MtG example
> > is not applicable to V:tES.
>
> I would rather identify a possible problem , analyze it and prevent
> it. The let us destroy a world so we can built it anew attitude is
> something I do not subscribe to.

It's not destroying the world to rebuilt it anew. It's a question of not
fixing things that aren't broken. If you go down that road, you never
discover whether the thing was ever going to become broken in the first
place. We don't know whether this will ever be broken because attempting
to use experience from Magic, as you are, is not valid.

Fred

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
jspektr wrote:

> What if the Camarilla set had contained around 40 new vampires,
> reprints of all the "good" Jyhad/VTES vampires, all of Dark Soveriegns
> and Ancient Hearts, and the unreprinted Sabbat edition vampires? Forty
> new camarilla vampires could probably have been designed in a way to
> not cause stacking problems with old vampires by giving them unusual
> discipline sets (which I think many old players enjoy, as it enables
> new and interesting decks). Then you'd have a base set with all the
> cards newbies supposedly can't get, without grouping.

I fail to see how this is preferable to the current system. Instead of 40
new vampires, we get 100 new vampires with which to build new crypts.
Different crypts. Just looking at the Nosferatu, if you want a Pot/Obf deck,
you stick with group 1/2 (using Nos and !Nos). If you wan't a Pot/Ani deck,
you use group 2/3 (using !Nos, Nos, and Raziya--a crypt revolving around
Raziya, Tommy, Nigel, and Amelia is going to be quite effective). If you
want a Pot/For Rush deck, you use group 2/3. If you want a Pot/For Prince
deck, you use group 1/2. There are now more options than there used to be
because of 100 new vampires, and we get to avoid:

A) The super optimized crypts that would come from each clan having 30
vampires.

B) New players from feeling like they *have* to get all the old, out of
print vampires to compete.

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:


I don't think the "brokeness" of unequal access to either cards in general or
vampires in particular is equivalent the brokeness of an individual unbalanced
card. But if you insist on comparing the two, then I'm saying in effect, unequal
access to cards - once a new player has gotten his collection up to a certain
reasonable size - is the equivalent of (pre-CE) Second Tradition, not Return to
Innocence. It's not completely fair, obviously. But is it unfair enough to
group cards? IMHO, not a chance. Especially not if you reprint key things to

applicable to library cards than to vampires since few or no vampires are the

or less, over all of them.)

Fred

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"Curevei" <cur...@aol.commetal> wrote in message
news:20021106125345...@mb-co.aol.com...

[Karol Magda wrote]

> >There are lot's of (potentially
> >good cards) which are not played that often because better
> >alternatives exists.
> >(and yes, it might be more problem with players not realizing subtle
> >benefits of
> >such cards compared to 'obvious' alternatives)
>
> I wouldn't call them good, since, by definition, in order to be good, a
card
> has to be desirable to play. But, yes, there are cards that would see
(more)
> play if better cards didn't exist.
>
> This is why I don't like seeing generic, high utility cards designed. I
once
> used to explain to people that: if you build three different decks with
> completely different strategies, it's a bad thing if a card to
automatically
> goes into all three decks; what is desired is for cards to be obvious for
one
> of the decks and useless in another.

This is true, I think. But I wonder if VTES doesn't by its structure
mostly squeeze all "strategies" into a fairly narrow space?

That is: all "strategies" must reduce their prey's pool to 0. Most
of them will have to bleed at some point to do this. All (or nearly
all) of them will use vampires of their own to accomplish it. Because
of these commonalities, things like Blood Doll tend to be useful for
every deck. If things like Blood Doll (totally generic cards, in the
game's "world", generally) didn't exist, there would certainly be less
commonality among the cards in decks. But if things like Blood Doll
(ways to move blood back from your vampires to your pool) didn't
exist, cards like Conditioning (+3 bleed for a single card and blood)
would be vastly more powerful than they already are (and they're
already very powerful).

That could be fine, if "games going fast" is something desirable and
the supremacy of fast-attack decks (or bounce etc) is generally
considered okay. But in a way, the existence of these "generic"
cards makes a lot of slower "strategies" more viable. (Scare quotes
because I'm not sure that they are truly different strategies in
the way you mean, Ian. Different methods, maybe, or flavors.)

Messages.Author: Joshua Duffin
Messages.Body:
"LSJ" <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in message
news:3DC98011...@white-wolf.com...

> The current design idea is that having a "level playing field" at the
> "any possible combination of <vampire> cards <ever to be> in existence"
> level is not satisfactory. Allowing everyone equal access to a broken
> system doesn't fix the system, it just means that everyone can abuse
> the system equally. Otherwise, why not just reprint Return to Innocence
> with the original text rather than errata'ing it and banning it?

I agree. But in the context of vampires, I'm not convinced that it's
possible to (within the bounds of reasonable adherence to the "point
system") have a more broken system than the one that's already in
existence.

We have - and will apparently always have - access to plenty of
Dominate, Presence, Obfuscate, Protean, Celerity, etc. weenies. If
it's possible for a profusion of midcaps and high-caps to be "more
broken" than this, I'd like to see evidence.

Josh

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:
>But if things like Blood Doll
>(ways to move blood back from your vampires to your pool) didn't
>exist, cards like Conditioning (+3 bleed for a single card and blood)
>would be vastly more powerful than they already are (and they're
>already very powerful).
>
>That could be fine, if "games going fast" is something desirable and
>the supremacy of fast-attack decks (or bounce etc) is generally
>considered okay. But in a way, the existence of these "generic"
>cards makes a lot of slower "strategies" more viable.

I'm all for eliminating Conditioning. Bleeding for a lot is way too easy, as
is hitting for a lot, stealthing for a lot, intercepting for a lot, passing
votes by a lot.

Not that I'd advocate eliminating Blood Doll, but Tribute is hardly useful in a
deck that puts out 1-2 vampires, Tap is hardly useful if you put out a bunch of
2 caps. Then, there's Powerbases, Blood Puppy, Slave Auction, Investments,
Ascendance, and whatever else. Blood Doll is just plain better than all of
them.

Messages.Author: jspektr
Messages.Body:
Snapcase <snap...@eudoramail.com> wrote in message news:<MPG.1832e1eb8...@news.optonline.net>...

> K, look at it this way. We've already got a boatload of cards that
> don't do what they say they do. It's part of the game, good or bad.
> Rehabilitating underpowered cards basically gives me free (and useful)
> cards. I like free, useful cards.

Maybe, but I have to agree with Fred. We constantly have problems with
cards that have been changed, and every game, EVERY GAME breaks down
at some point when someone has to stop and check a card to see what
the text has been changed to and whether clarifications/errata have
been issued on it. It's incredibly irritating, and turns off new
players.

If White Wolf is going to change card texts, I think they should then
reprint the changed cards, and make them available for a small fee
from the White Wolf website. Like packs of 10 2nd Traditions with the
new text for $1. Otherwise, text should only be changed if the card is
having a serious detrimental impact, like Return to Innocence.

JSpektr

Messages.Author: Gomi no Sensei
Messages.Body:
In article <aqc33k$8ohfq$1...@id-121616.news.dfncis.de>,
Joshua Duffin <jtdu...@yahoo.com> wrote:

>That is: all "strategies" must reduce their prey's pool to 0. Most
>of them will have to bleed at some point to do this. All (or nearly
>all) of them will use vampires of their own to accomplish it. Because
>of these commonalities, things like Blood Doll tend to be useful for
>every deck. If things like Blood Doll (totally generic cards, in the
>game's "world", generally) didn't exist, there would certainly be less

>commonality among the cards in decks. But if things like Blood Doll

>(ways to move blood back from your vampires to your pool) didn't
>exist, cards like Conditioning (+3 bleed for a single card and blood)
>would be vastly more powerful than they already are (and they're
>already very powerful).

What I'd like to see is different ways of accomplishing goals -- the
new combat options (Tension in the Ranks) plus existing Fame let combat
decks get somewhere here, and vote decks don't _have_ to bleed to remove
pool, of course. But what I'd really like is more options for gaining
pool that aren't master cards. A 'strike: gain 1 pool' seems really
in-character for Ravnos/CHI, for instance, or a financier ally that
can take an action to gain 1 pool, or other ways -- because pool
replenishment tends to eat up a third to half to all my master slots in
decks these days, and I'd sure like to use those scarce master phases
for things that are more fun.

GtU-based bloat, f'rinstance, is pretty viable with a Crypt-Machine
kind of approach, and GtU's versatility is one of the things that makes
it such a staple.

Other things I wouldn't mind seeing is more special-case bleed actions,
like a THA or AUS 'bleed at -1 bleed, bounces cost 1 more blood' or
wacky specials like Propaganda. Action modifiers on successful (D)
or even non-(D) actions to burn a pool/blood. Wacky shit like that.

And, as Ian mentions, things for Celerity/Potence to do that aren't
combat. That would be super neat.

gomi
portentous celery
--
Everybody's playing the game
But nobody's rules are the same

They have been making comparable critters to Juzam for years, actually.
Juzam is just a poor example of a power card. Mana Drain will do,
though.

> Extended still allowed multilands last I looked. They stopped printing multilands
> and proceeded to design cards after 4th edition as if multilands didn't exist. At
> some point, extended will lop of all the base sets and expansions that included

This has happened fairly recently and indeed has resulted in a more

> Even now, however, if they print an overpowered that's not absolutely gamebreaking,
> they don't bother to errata it or ban it or anything. They just let it sit there and
> fester, causing a number of other cards to be much less useful because they don't
> measure up to a game filled with top-of-the-heap power cards.

Part of this reason is that the cards will rotate out of type 2 in a
relatively short period of time. Also, Wizards has a habit of printing
a card or series of cards in future expansions to hose the old card that
was at the top of the power curve.

> That's unfortunate, but
> it still doesn't help to ignore a real problem that exists and pretend T1.5
> is balanced in its current form. It isn't. Not even close.

Completely true, but there are *many* broken strategies in type 1.5; at
least it's not a stagnant imbalance. And really, there are no
sanctioned 1.5 tournaments anymore. Wizards doesn't have the need to
balance it, because nobody's playing it (and it doesn't bring them any
new business).

> > So grouping library cards would actually make more of your cards
> > playable in the long run. I can't see why it is bad thing.
>
> It's a bad thing because 1) it's not necessary, 2) it's too complicated, and
> 3) it clearly annoys people.

Amen on #3. It's pretty much the reason I stopped playing magic. It
wasn't the cost of keeping up as much as the fact that being forced to
start over every year just wasn't very interesting anymore. If I had a
neat deck that I liked in type 2 it was obsoleted in a year (sometimes
as little time as 5 months, depending on what set combinations the key
cards came from). Sure, it was still legal in Extended but it wasn't
competitive.

The way Wizards has structured the tournament scene, card groupings
cause less of your cards to be playable in the long run. Type 2 is the
most common tournament by far, extended less so, with 1.5 being
nonexistent. Would White Wolf fall into the same trap? Unknown. I'd
rather not be forced to find out.

-Snapcase

> > > Over time, continuing to add more and more new cards should not cause

>

Messages.Author: agzocgud
Messages.Body:
For the really bad cards you can make combo-cards.
Example:

"Monsters from the past" combines Legacy of Caine, Anachronism and
Fear of Mekhet into one card. When you play the card you choose one of
the three effects.

The method works only on certain cards, but masters can be dealt with
this way. When was the last time you saw "The Damned" in play? Combine
it with some other minor effects and you have a flexible card that
works against younger vampires.
("Under preassure: >4 cap is tapped & doesn´t untap during next
untap"; "Questionable Lineage: >4 cap becomes clanless & indepedent")

For the really good cards there are four ways to go.
Ban, restrict, errata or print a nullifier. All four of them are lame,
but I think that a restriction is the least bad option. No, I don´t
play with a cardlimit. No, I´m not a fascist.
But I wouldn´t mind if you only were allowed 3-5 2nd & 5th, for
example. (old versions)

/Mathias

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
agzocgud wrote:
> For the really good cards there are four ways to go.
> Ban, restrict, errata or print a nullifier. All four of them are lame,
> but I think that a restriction is the least bad option.

I think it's clearly the worst option. Admit a card is overpowered but
allow _some_ copies? So you're allowing _some_ overpowered cards in each
game? On top of which, when and if they come up in the deck makes for
a swing of luck since if they don't, you have to rely on your "mundane"
cards to carry you through...

Fred

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:


It might not be the "worst" option if the card was only overpowered when
played in multiples with itself. Putting it on a restricted list whereby
only 1 could be in a deck would "fix" the card (neuter it) more severely
than adding errata to say "a minion can play only 1 <X> each <time period>".

Not that there's any plan to make a restricted list currently, of course.



I haven't looked in on it in two years. I have a few specific details wrong (which
I already conceded were suspect) but so what? Please address how this affects the
overall issue. Simply finding an incorrect statement that doesn't alter the
underpinnings of the other person's argument is irrelevant.

To the extent Extended has become "fair", it has also turned into a slow-moving T2
that bans whole expansions and editions of the base set at a time. So it can not be
seen as a good example for another CCG to emulate. Your cards rotate through states:
being legal for all tournaments, being legal for Extended, T1, and T1.5, then only
for T1 and T1.5 at some point. Unless reprinted, they then become effectively useless
as no one wants to play unbalanced T1 OR T1.5. This is one of the reasons I stopped
playing Magic.

> > > Hovewer almost no-brainer cards do exists in V:TES , one classic
> > > example would be a blood doll (and I am not saying it is broken, I am just saying

> > can use it.
>
> So what if I call all broken / powerfull cards 'staple' ?

What if you do? Is anyone going to believe you? Does your "staple" lend itself
to a making one easy, obvious deck that tends to dominate the game or does it get
used as a building block in lots of completely different types of decks? Was its
effect clearly intended by the designers or did its use (particularly in combination
with one or a small number of other cards) seem to surprise them?

It's not always cut and dried whether a card is a "staple" or a broken card. But
usually there are fairly obvious clues to discern the two different situations.
The bottom line is whether it seems to help or hurt the game as a whole.

> > Magic could be fixed, too, if the DCI had a desire to do so.
>
> There is desire in both DCI and R&D, don't make no mistake.

No, I mean if they had a DESIRE to. Like, if they cared more about making the
game balanced than not getting flamed a bunch of people who don't understand
game balance issues. One difference between the Magic newsgroup and this one:
you mention game balance here and most everyone understands what you're talking
about. Bring up the issue in the Magic newsgroup and there's still a bunch of
people who are clueless about it and will not accept it as a reason for doing
anything with the game. They care only about other things, such as promoting
the type of deck they like to play and making sure their collection remains as
powerful and monetarily valuable as possible. I don't fault such motivations.
But many of them don't seem to understand that if you don't have game balance,
ultimately, you have a lousy game.

The DCI, for one reason or another, has never been able to stand up and take
care of the balance problems in T1.5. (And who even cares about T1?) They
refuse to use errata and they don't want to take responsibility for banning
cards. The result is a format nobody plays. So cards rotated out of Extended
have no place to go unless/until they happen to get reprinted.

> > > > standard in terms of balance in general. So even in a single set even in

> > >
> > > I do believe that Magic is far more balanced than it was say two or

>

> where designers talk about things they do and WHY they do it.

I didn't say anything about being literally dishonest with their reasoning. I said
being totally honest about overpowered old cards and what truly needs to be done
about them. I mean I do think the DCI has some concept of balancing the game,
they just can't bring themselves to the inevitable, indisputable conclusion that
if they wouldn't print an old card in this year's expansion because it is now
considered too powerful, then they shouldn't allow it in its original form in
T1.5. To me, that seems obvious. Why the DCI can't see that is perplexing.

> What I am saying that adding new cards to the system will walpaperize
> some cards in process no matter how would you like to prevent it (why
> should I play with pokers in my !Salubri when there is weighted
> walking stick in format ?)

I don't understand the question. The two cards clearly have their differences
and you might choose to use either, depending on whether you care how easy the
weapon is to put into play, how quickly it goes away and whether you're more
likely to see Fortitude damage prevention or Kiaysd vampires in your metagame.
Clearly, Weighted Walking Stick does not "wallpaperize" Poker. It simply
provides another alternative that does the same thing with somewhat different
specifics.

I think you need to come up with a different example to express your question.

> > > Would you thing that some of the following things would be good for
> > > the game:
> > >
> > > 1)printing 5 more aus/AUS intercept cards
> > > 2)printing 5 more obf/OBF stealth cards

Sure. So what? Not all the time. And even if so, all you've done is

problem, per se.

> > > 7)printing more presence bleed cards
>

> > too bad. I agree it's bad if it happens. But if such cards are too
> > bad, you've wasted some cardboard. If they're too good, then that's
> > when errata things.
>
> If they are bad - wallpaper printed, point proven.
> If they are good - old card wallpaperized, point proven.

Those are mistakes in design. If they are bad, they are ignored, which is
not a problem. If they are good, as I said, they will get errata or get
banned. Also not a problem. I don't know what your point could be. This
does not cause the overall problem you claimed.

> > > 4)printing some more ANI intercept cards
> > > 5)printing some more free OBT stealth cards

> > > 4),5) - the entire balance between disciplines would be throwed out of

> >
> > It could be. You can simply reprint the existing free OBT stealth cards

> > issue, either.
>

> create less incentive for old players to buy (parts) of new set.

So? That situation already exists. We already have reprints in sets. There
are ways to reprint cards that tend to funnel them into places that they can
have little or no effect on new card sales. Put them precons. Reprint in
sets like Camarilla Edition that are intended mainly for new players (and get
rid of most or all new cards in such sets). Or reprint few enough cards in
boosters intended to release new cards that old players won't care very much.
I believe you're struggling to insist that there's a problem here but there
isn't. It has a reasonably easy alternative solution. And I suggest another
alternative solution below (i.e. the Elder Intervention/Pack Tactics and
bleed modifier types of solutions).

> Although I feel that reprints are necessary (in current state, since
> game is just being reintroduced to larger audience) they are quite
> boring.

Sure. That's why White Wolf should try to isolate them to places that new
players can buy and you can ignore.

> I desperately want to see new cards for old disciplines. If that
> didn't happen soon, I am afraid the game will become too dull for me
> soon :(

Sure. You can have new cards for old disciplines. There's nothing here that
prevents it. Your last example, about discipline balance issues with respect
to a limitation in named cards that will do a certain thing (e.g. free stealth
for obtenebration) may place limitations on designing a few sorts of isolated
things but so what? Even that has an answer. Notice what they did for Elder
Intervention and Pack Tactics? They didn't want two disciplineless +2 intercept
cards allowed to react to the same bleed action. So they just wrote it straight
out: you may not use both cards against the same action. Notice what they do
for bleed modifiers. They have lots of different named bleed action modifiers
that do different things but you can only use one of them in a given action
anyway (excepting the case of Command of the Beast). Your issues have other
solutions aside from grouping library cards.

> > > So what do you suggest ? Banning 100 most abusive cards in the game ?
> > > Guess what ? Even after that another 100 most abusive cards appear.
> >
> > That's the old Magic newsgroup refrain, isn't it? My reply to it is invariable:
> > cards that are randomly distributed in terms of what can loosely be called,

>
> What if power level of cards has different distribution ? What then ?
> Entire construction out of window.

It doesn't have a different distribution. There's no reason it should.

> > Rather than banning cards, of course, you can errata them. WotC goes to the
> > other side of errata fanaticism: they almost entirely refuse to do it at all,
> > ever. That's their choice but regardless of which choice they make, it's much
> > better than simply ignoring the problem which they've done. And yes, in T1.5,
> > a *lot* of cards would need to be dealt with. Dozens, maybe over a hundred,

> Actually when I talked with one of my friend who does not play CCG
> anymore about how things WotC do ( no errata, rather phasing it out and
> printing lesser version) and how things WW do (errata when card is too
> powerfull) he considered WotC approach better one. So I guess it's

It is a matter of taste, I suppose. But the results speak for themselves. No
one is satisfied with the end result in Magic. People leave the game inevitably
because they consider it to be a huge money sucker that ultimately leaves them

> everything else in the "card universe") should come into here
> somewhere. Return to Innocence would still be annoying if it were
> common, right? And Disarm?

Disarm would be fine. Just overprinted I suspect. I was responding
to Karol Magda about this elsewhere in this thread. To me, "stapleness"
implies a designer-intended common utility effect that itself doesn't
constrain overall strategy. Return to Innocence could be a staple
if the game had been designed around letting vampires burn themselves to
effect large bleeds. If so, the game would need to branch out into a
number of alternative substrategies within that reality, or else provide
alternative strategies that were as powerful and/or somehow could turn
RtI against itself. (Bounce actually does that somewhat but bounce
itself is deemed too narrow to be considered an answer.) Were this true,
it could reasonably be thought of as a staple. Then it probably shouldn't
be a rare, of course. But none of this is true. So it's overpowered.

This is why I say, commonality isn't really proof that a card is or isn't
a staple. It's just that if a card truly functions as a staple, it
_should_ be common because it's going to be used to effect many different
strategies.

Another clue, by the way, involves whether the card was originally printed
in a base set. Although in rare cases, certain cards get printed in
expansions that ultimately become staples (at least sort of) because they
drop into the game so nicely. Carrion Crows is a good example of this because
it became such a nice partner to Aid From Bats and animalism really needed the
combat option. Normally, though, most staples were created in the beginning
and the game has "grown up" around them. So it's unlikely that an expansion
rare is going to qualify. A card is an expansion rare because it was thought
of as a highly specialized card to begin with. Trying to justify a card like
that as a "staple" would be like uprooting a tree and planting it by one the
end of one of its outside branches. The tree is gonna look kind of funny
that way...and probably not stand up very well.

Fred

Personally, I've been doing this, and not playing with any changed
cards. Unfortunately, in a competitive environment, that rules out
many decks. I have a Daughters of Cacophony deck I'm working on for
the Eye of Overpowered Cheese tournament, and it just flat-out doesn't
work well enough without Majesty. Ditto my Eurobrujah deck and 2nd
Tradition/Thoughts Betrayed/Fame.

It has been fun to be forced to play unusual decks, I've been doing a
lot of Tzemisce, because most Animalism/Auspex/Vissiccitude cards
haven't been changed. But it is not a limitation I would prefer to
have.

Also, like Fred said, your opponents frequently play cards with
incorrect text. That causes a huge problem you can't control.

The problem is worse for newbies and players without net access. Last
night, an older player that had just returned to the game had his
entire deck ruined because several cards he'd based it around no
longer did what they said. He was a good sport about it, but how does
this help us bring back old players? Should we just tell them "too
bad, White Wolf hates you and doesn't want your business, all your old
stuff doesn't work anymore and there was no way for you to know about
it"?

When I came back to the game last fall, I didn't even know White Wolf
was reprinting cards. It's not as if they advertise, or put up posters
in comic shops, at least not around here. Old and new players aren't
going to know about the errata, and it is going to hurt the game when
they are surprised by it. The best solution I can think of is to stop
issuing card text changes unless absolutely necessary, and to included
a list of all changes in the rule books in the starters, even if that
means doubling the size of the rule book.

JSpektr

> > > then it would change the game over time.
> >
> > Most of the time, what you need is different intercept cards.
>
> Sure. So what? Not all the time. And even if so, all you've done is
> change the game a bit by adding more variety. That's not evidence of a
> problem, per se.

No, some game principles (which are there for good reason, I believe)
would be made obsolete.

> > > > 3)printing 5 more for/FOR prevent cards
> > > > 6)printing more dominate bleed cards
> > > > 7)printing more presence bleed cards
>
> > > > 3),6),7) - the cards would be too good or too bad compared to what we
> > > > have in their categories now. Both options are not good.
> > >
> > > It isn't clear to me that such cards would necessarily be too good or
> > > too bad. I agree it's bad if it happens. But if such cards are too
> > > bad, you've wasted some cardboard. If they're too good, then that's
> > > when errata things.
> >
> > If they are bad - wallpaper printed, point proven.
> > If they are good - old card wallpaperized, point proven.

> Those are mistakes in design. If they are bad, they are ignored, which is
> not a problem. If they are good, as I said, they will get errata or get
> banned. Also not a problem. I don't know what your point could be. This
> does not cause the overall problem you claimed.

No, that's an inherent problem of adding (many) new cards to the
system.

> > > > 4)printing some more ANI intercept cards
> > > > 5)printing some more free OBT stealth cards
>
> > > > 4),5) - the entire balance between disciplines would be throwed out of
> > > > window in process
> > >
> > > It could be. You can simply reprint the existing free OBT stealth cards
> > > or ANI intercept cards in future expansions if it's the designers' intent
> > > to limit the number of different named cards. So this is not really an
> > > issue, either.
> >
> > It is, you don't get new cards in that category and therefore you will
> > create less incentive for old players to buy (parts) of new set.

> So? That situation already exists. We already have reprints in sets. There
> are ways to reprint cards that tend to funnel them into places that they can
> have little or no effect on new card sales. Put them precons. Reprint in
> sets like Camarilla Edition that are intended mainly for new players (and get
> rid of most or all new cards in such sets). Or reprint few enough cards in
> boosters intended to release new cards that old players won't care very much.
> I believe you're struggling to insist that there's a problem here but there
> isn't. It has a reasonably easy alternative solution. And I suggest another
> alternative solution below (i.e. the Elder Intervention/Pack Tactics and
> bleed modifier types of solutions).

Reprints only solve problem partially (that acess to most of the old
cards is difficult for new players). As new cards are printed some
parts of old players collection will become obsolete.

> > Although I feel that reprints are necessary (in current state, since
> > game is just being reintroduced to larger audience) they are quite
> > boring.
>
> Sure. That's why White Wolf should try to isolate them to places that new
> players can buy and you can ignore.

> > I desperately want to see new cards for old disciplines. If that
> > didn't happen soon, I am afraid the game will become too dull for me
> > soon :(

> Sure. You can have new cards for old disciplines. There's nothing here that
> prevents it. Your last example, about discipline balance issues with respect
> to a limitation in named cards that will do a certain thing (e.g. free stealth
> for obtenebration) may place limitations on designing a few sorts of isolated
> things but so what? Even that has an answer. Notice what they did for Elder
> Intervention and Pack Tactics? They didn't want two disciplineless +2 intercept
> cards allowed to react to the same bleed action. So they just wrote it straight
> out: you may not use both cards against the same action. Notice what they do
> for bleed modifiers. They have lots of different named bleed action modifiers
> that do different things but you can only use one of them in a given action
> anyway (excepting the case of Command of the Beast). Your issues have other
> solutions aside from grouping library cards.

Elder Intervention and Pack Tactics is nice example why grouping is
good. Same goes for action modifier example. Notice that another
solution would be to print little number somewhere on the card. Saved
place (in card text), could be used for something better then.

Rather then adding stupid lines of text which would eventually appear
on many cards (and in long run would cause great confusion) why not
rather implement much robust system ?

> > > > So what do you suggest ? Banning 100 most abusive cards in the game ?
> > > > Guess what ? Even after that another 100 most abusive cards appear.
> > >
> > > That's the old Magic newsgroup refrain, isn't it? My reply to it is invariable:
> > > cards that are randomly distributed in terms of what can loosely be called,
> > > "power". This distribution is a classic bell-shaped curve in which the most
> > > powerful cards are a relative few located at the top of the curve. Lop off
> > > this thin "tip" of the curve and other cards will, indeed become "the most
> > > powerful". However, once you've lopped off enough of the tip, the cards left
> > > on top are only a little bit more powerful than most of the rest of the cards
> > > in the middle. At that point, the game is now much better because it's much
> > > harder to choose the best cards and strategies. Life is now good.
> >
> > What if power level of cards has different distribution ? What then ?
> > Entire construction out of window.
>
> It doesn't have a different distribution. There's no reason it should.

I doesn't have to have different distribution. Normal distribution
(with different parameters than classic bell curve you are suggesting)
would be sufficient for counterexample.

> > > Rather than banning cards, of course, you can errata them. WotC goes to the
> > > other side of errata fanaticism: they almost entirely refuse to do it at all,
> > > ever. That's their choice but regardless of which choice they make, it's much
> > > better than simply ignoring the problem which they've done. And yes, in T1.5,
> > > a *lot* of cards would need to be dealt with. Dozens, maybe over a hundred,
> > > just because they printed so many cards before the idea of game balance
> > > penetrated the thick skulls of the Magic design team. That's unfortunate, but
> > > it still doesn't help to ignore a real problem that exists and pretend T1.5
> > > is balanced in its current form. It isn't. Not even close.
> >
> > Actually when I talked with one of my friend who does not play CCG
> > anymore about how things WotC do ( no errata, rather phasing it out and
> > printing lesser version) and how things WW do (errata when card is too
> > powerfull) he considered WotC approach better one. So I guess it's
> > matter of taste. (note: I do prefer WW approach, but I can understand
> > the other one)
>
> It is a matter of taste, I suppose. But the results speak for themselves. No
> one is satisfied with the end result in Magic. People leave the game inevitably
> because they consider it to be a huge money sucker that ultimately leaves them
> with far too many dead cards for various reasons.

The game as a whole survives, and gets better as times goes on
(despite people leaving for one reason or another)

> Be that as it may, the overall point I was making was that the two approaches
> were different. Whether you consider the White Wolf approach superior not is
> orthogonal to the conclusion that grouping library cards are not necessary to
> answer a potential problem in V:tES that you see in Magic. Since the same
> conditions do not apply in V:tES as in Magic, you can't claim that the same
> eventual problem will occur.

Actually the problem is inherent to each CCG. Adding new cards to
current card set (without limiting their interaction in some way) will
walpaperize old some old cards and will cause some new cards not to be
even played.

> > > > The number of cards played in given format is some percentage of
> > > > number of cards in format. The greater the number of cards in format ,
> > > > the smaller the percentage.
> > >
> > > I disagree.
> >
> > Care to say why?
>
> I already have: because overpowered cards are fixed in V:tES whereas they're
> allowed to fester in Magic.

Every archetype out there is built from some sub-pool of the avaiable
cards. If you add more cards to that sub-pool some old cards will not
be used anymore. It's that simple.

> > > > So grouping library cards would actually make more of your cards
> > > > playable in the long run. I can't see why it is bad thing.
> > >
> > > It's a bad thing because 1) it's not necessary, 2) it's too complicated, and
> > > 3) it clearly annoys people.
> >
> > 1) we have precedence
> > 2) ditto
>
> So? Precedence is not a reason to do something if it was a bad thing. And
> whatever you may think of grouping vampires, again, the same conditions do
> not apply to library cards so the same answer is not necessary.
>
> > 3) So what ? The product is not aimed at people who cries sky is
> > falling everytime something annoys them.
>
> Annoying people is a bad thing to do if you don't have a good reason to do it.
> I'll accept bad things if you have a greater good thing come from it. But you
> haven't shown anything good would come from grouping library cards.

3) we have precedence :)

The conditions with library grouping are quite similar (or they will
be if there would be some vast influx of library cards to classic
disciplines (the ones they appeared in jyhad) )

> (Elided several questions I've already answered.)
>
> > > > > > Grouping of library cards would open vast posibilities for new cards
> > > > > > and abilities which do have an impact and are not broken (and it may
> > > > > > become a problem otherwise in (not so) distant future)
> > > > >
> > > > > It is unlikely to become a problem. At least, let it become a true
> > > > > problem and then we can evaluate what to do about it. The MtG example
> > > > > is not applicable to V:tES.
> > > >
> > > > I would rather identify a possible problem , analyze it and prevent
> > > > it. The let us destroy a world so we can built it anew attitude is
> > > > something I do not subscribe to.
> > >
> > > It's not destroying the world to rebuilt it anew. It's a question of not
> > > fixing things that aren't broken. If you go down that road, you never
> > > discover whether the thing was ever going to become broken in the first
> > > place. We don't know whether this will ever be broken because attempting
> > > to use experience from Magic, as you are, is not valid.
> >
> > I don't saw any point made that would made my example not valid.
> > Sorry.
>
> I guess we'll have to disagree about that.

Sure.

> You've essentially conceded that the
> philosophies of the designers of the two different game clearly differ in terms
> of handling overpowered cards. Some of the other issues you brought up are
> either irrelevant and/or have better answers than grouping library cards.
> Inevitably, people will vary in how they look at complex issues such as these.
> But I think the case for group library cards at this point is extremely weak.

And (even if I did) so what ? The problem is not about handling
overpowered cards (or is only partialy). The problem is that adding
new cards while keeping old cards in format cause -

1) format to be impossible to balance
2) wallpaperization of old cards
3) insignificance of new cards
4) creates BIG advantage to old or new players (depending whether 2 or
3 is prevalent)
5) make old players quit and new players scared

All of this issues could be solved differently that grouping, yes.
This solutions does not adress those problems that nicely as grouping
does. Therefore I think that grouping solution is quite robust.

Karol

Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
Fred writes:

>A few people seem to have trouble with the concept that a massive
>amount of errata could be that bad for the game because they insist on
>looking at it from the standpoint of how minor a single instance is.
>I am attempting to demonstrate why leaning on this tool too much over
>time actually causes a serious problem.

Originally I was thrilled about card rehabilitation but now I'm having
second thoughts. We have 2 new players coming this week and I
dread having to explain to them "oh, I know this card SAYS this
but it really does..." Reining in cards like Majesty is important enough
we have to deal with it but Blood Puppy could have stayed as it
was (ie, in my folder :-)

I can see why WW would want to do this though; it's another
attempt to be fair to existing card owners and not force them
onto the buying treadmill. If they had added a CE "Blood Poopy"
card which worked the way the errata'd BP did, all us old hands
would be at a disadvantage. They way they do it now maximizes
the ability of old players to stay in without buying more. So,
as usual, there are tradeoffs.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)
"It is better to be wrong than to be vague" - Freeman Dyson

> this help us bring back old players? Should we just tell them "too
> bad, White Wolf hates you and doesn't want your business, all your old
> stuff doesn't work anymore and there was no way for you to know about
> it"?

Well, if you like the game and want it to continue to succeed, I
wouldn't recommend saying that, no. You might instead try something
like "White Wolf decided that game balance was crucial to keeping
the game interesting, so they changed a lot of cards that they
determined to be overpowered as originally printed." :-)

> When I came back to the game last fall, I didn't even know White Wolf
> was reprinting cards. It's not as if they advertise, or put up posters
> in comic shops, at least not around here. Old and new players aren't
> going to know about the errata, and it is going to hurt the game when
> they are surprised by it. The best solution I can think of is to stop
> issuing card text changes unless absolutely necessary, and to included
> a list of all changes in the rule books in the starters, even if that
> means doubling the size of the rule book.

That's a really good idea, I think. Putting the complete "card text
migrations" webpage in the rulebook would be really helpful in (a)
providing an easily-portable reference that people might actually have
with them whenever playing and (b) getting the word out to people who
aren't already WW-website-aware. (It'd be almost like Fred's "The
Book!")

Josh

First of all, that's a clearly subjective opinion. Other people might see it

Huh?!? Please back up and explain the logic behind that statement. Elder
Intervention and Pack Tactics is an example of how to solve the problem
you cited _without_ doing something drastic like grouping. So how do you
figure it's a "nice example why grouping is good".

> > > > > So what do you suggest ? Banning 100 most abusive cards in the game ?
> > > > > Guess what ? Even after that another 100 most abusive cards appear.
> > > >
> > > > That's the old Magic newsgroup refrain, isn't it? My reply to it is invariable:
> > > > cards that are randomly distributed in terms of what can loosely be called,
> > > > "power". This distribution is a classic bell-shaped curve in which the most
> > > > powerful cards are a relative few located at the top of the curve. Lop off
> > > > this thin "tip" of the curve and other cards will, indeed become "the most
> > > > powerful". However, once you've lopped off enough of the tip, the cards left
> > > > on top are only a little bit more powerful than most of the rest of the cards
> > > > in the middle. At that point, the game is now much better because it's much
> > > > harder to choose the best cards and strategies. Life is now good.
> > >
> > > What if power level of cards has different distribution ? What then ?
> > > Entire construction out of window.
> >
> > It doesn't have a different distribution. There's no reason it should.
>
> I doesn't have to have different distribution. Normal distribution
> (with different parameters than classic bell curve you are suggesting)
> would be sufficient for counterexample.

I suppose. So it might work or it might not, depending on what you think the
distribution curve of the power cards looks like. But your original assertion was
that banning "100 most abusive cards" will cause another 100 "most abusive" cards
to appear. I explained why I thought banning or issuing errata to the most abusive
cards DOES work and doesn't simply cause the situation you fear. I believe Scott
Johnson has SHOWN that it works, given how much the game improved after the 7/7
errata he issued a few year ago. People complained a great deal but the result was
undeniably a better game. Abusive cards were NOT replaced by other cards that were
equally abusive. You can believe it or you can refuse to believe it but I think
the evidence speaks for itself. In fact, my only quibble with it was whether he
went to far and issued more errata than he had to to fix the game.

(More non-new arguments elided)
...

> > You've essentially conceded that the
> > philosophies of the designers of the two different game clearly differ in terms
> > of handling overpowered cards. Some of the other issues you brought up are
> > either irrelevant and/or have better answers than grouping library cards.
> > Inevitably, people will vary in how they look at complex issues such as these.
> > But I think the case for group library cards at this point is extremely weak.
>

> And (even if I did) so what? The problem is not about handling

> overpowered cards (or is only partialy). The problem is that adding
> new cards while keeping old cards in format cause -
>
> 1) format to be impossible to balance
> 2) wallpaperization of old cards
> 3) insignificance of new cards
> 4) creates BIG advantage to old or new players (depending whether 2 or
> 3 is prevalent)
> 5) make old players quit and new players scared

I disagree that any of these are true in V:tES. They are true in Magic
BECAUSE of the differences in the designers' handling of overpowered cards
in each game. The *MTG* T1 and T1.5 formats are impossible to balance because
the *MTG* designers refuse to ban or errata cards that are overpowered unless
the card in question reaches an unnecessarily high level of perniciousness.
Remove that policy and I believe you'll find that T1.5 can be balanced, that
new cards do not routinely wallpaperize old cards, nor visa versa. Absent
(1), (2), and (3), you will then find that old players needn't have nearly
as large an advantage over new players in T1.5 once the new players collect
a fairly reasonable number of cards. Since old players don't have the huge
advantage, T2 needn't be the "standard" format it is now. It can become a
format for new players to play in until their collections become large enough
to compete reasonably well with older players. Given THAT, in turn, the
standard format would become T1.5 and it would become a very popular format.
Therefore, older players needn't feel that newer players have an advantage,
either.

It all works. The reason I don't play Magic anymore is twofold: the DCI
refuses to fix T1.5 and make is useful, as the could; and 2) WotC issues
too many expansions every year causing poor card design and costing me
too much money to keep up. Slow down the expansions and I think you'll
find THAT helps avoid card imbalance - leading to all these good results
I cited about above as well.

Fred

(Concerning Karol's assertion that, "Banning the 100 most abusive cards in the game
will only cause another 100 cards to become 'abusive'" and my reply that the normal
distribution of power in cards will assure that this is not an endless cycle. He
replies that this depends on what the normal distribution of power in cards truly
looks like. I replied:)

> > I suppose. So it might work or it might not, depending on what you think the
> > distribution curve of the power cards looks like. But your original assertion was
> > that banning "100 most abusive cards" will cause another 100 "most abusive" cards
> > to appear. I explained why I thought banning or issuing errata to the most abusive
> > cards DOES work and doesn't simply cause the situation you fear. I believe Scott
> > Johnson has SHOWN that it works, given how much the game improved after the 7/7
> > errata he issued a few year ago. People complained a great deal but the result was
> > undeniably a better game. Abusive cards were NOT replaced by other cards that were
> > equally abusive. You can believe it or you can refuse to believe it but I think
> > the evidence speaks for itself. In fact, my only quibble with it was whether he
> > went to far and issued more errata than he had to to fix the game.
>
> Counterexample #1 - after restriction of Black Vise new power cards
> like Land Tax or Necropotence were abused.
>
> Counterexample #2 - recent CE erratas of some power cards (or MRP
> curse to be exact)

Why are you giving counterexamples? Counterexamples prove nothing. I already
conceded, "It might work or it might not." Counterexamples don't prove something can
*never* work. They can only prove that the thing *sometimes* doesn't work.

In this case, I assert these counterexamples don't even prove *THAT*: 1) Magic examples,
as I've stated many times don't apply. The DCI doesn't ban all abusive cards anyway
so who cares what happens in Magic? Black Vise was abusive, Land Tax was abusive, and
Necropotence was abusive. In this case, the problem is that the DIC just didn't ban
enough cards to get near the point of fixing the problem. Doesn't mean the problem
couldn't be fixed. It just means the DCI wasn't willing to do what truly needed to be
done. 2) I don't agree that recent CE erratas of power cards were necessary, anyway.
That the V:tES designers seem a bit over finicky about the slightly more powerful cards
says nothing about the generally principle that's in dispute. And even if they were
necessary, who said there were any more abusive cards?

> > The reason I don't play Magic anymore is twofold: the DCI
> > refuses to fix T1.5 and make is useful, as the could; and 2) WotC issues
> > too many expansions every year causing poor card design and costing me
> > too much money to keep up. Slow down the expansions and I think you'll
> > find THAT helps avoid card imbalance - leading to all these good results
> > I cited about above as well.
>
> Look. T1.5 have like 10 000 of cards. Most of the cards can interact
> with themselves one way or another. Just compute the number of
> two/three/four cards combos. (waiting for him to do so....) See, big
> number isn't it ? Well and any of this combo can be really abusive.
> How can you prevent it from happening ?

You stay alert to it as you design the cards. Part of the problem is that
Magic designers are careless and put out expansions far too quickly to properly
balance cards. And when they do make mistakes, they leave them in the game
as is instead of fixing them. So *of course* you get problems like this.

The other thing I've touched on is the issue of combinations in Magic. Due
to the fact that Magic is 4CL, the designers way of balancing combinations is
to make sure most combination cards don't work well as single cards. Then they
count on the fact that it's hard to get a combination of cards into play reliably.
In the short run, this seems to work well enough. In the long run, they don't
pay enough attention to how much payoff a given combination provides - so the
issue comes up time and again in T1.5. Jyhad designers are much more sensitive
to how combinations of cards could possibly work because there are no card
limits in Jyhad.

> If we want to balance say tsimisce we have to take into account about
> 100 ani/aus/vic/tsimisce cards and about 400 ? relevant generic cards.
> We had to prevent abusive combos within this category at least and
> make it balanced with similar 15? or so subsystems. Not that easy
> task, but still manageable.
> Now imagine we had say 10 more cards in each subsystem.

You do it by setting limits on what any single card is allowed to do in various
respects. In Magic, one card is frequently worthless by itself but changes the
rules of the game completely: for instance the way Moat does nothing directly
for you but makes non-Flying creatures irrelevant as long as it's in play. Cards
like that are dangerous over time. I believe the Jyhad designers are much more
careful about such things.

It generally isn't necessary that you directly compare every card to every other
card to expose problems with combinations if you're careful about what kind of
cards you allow to be designed. Or at least, it lessens the chance that an error
will occur if you're careful. And if you do make a mistake, it can be fixed.
Without grouping.

Fred

> like Land Tax or Necropotence were abused.

We're talking Type 1 here now? Necropotence had its place in a few
decks, but it certainly didn't get overused until the Donate/Delusions
fiasco. Land Tax is a mediocre card in a format where few decks can
utilize basic lands (you'll note that it's neither restricted or
banned). Both don't mean as much in a format where Timetwister,
Ancestral and Wheel of Fortune are legal. These cards didn't have their
usefulness shoot through the roof when Vice got restricted/banned, the
entire deckstyle that wanted to play them did. Black Vice
singlehandedly prevented the slower/draw more cards control deckstyle.
When you can do six to nine damage on the first turn by dropping
multiple vices in their face, to a deck that wants to slow down and
control the game, you've basically won before they even hit their first
draw step. Especially when their deckstyle plays into getting hit more
by the vices.

> two/three/four cards combos. (waiting for him to do so....) See, big
> number isn't it ? Well and any of this combo can be really abusive.
> How can you prevent it from happening ?

Quite simply, by designing the cards more carefully.
Type 1 and 1.5 have become *more* broken over the years because Wizards
DOES NOT LOOK at those formats when designing new cards. They haven't
cared about them since they printed Ice Age and introduced type 2. They
print whatever cards they want to make Type 2 a fast-selling format, and
worry about restricting or banning them from the older formats later.

Examples?

> and power escalation will be present.

How is power escalation present in the current environment? What new
cards have been made that have immediately gone to the top of the
power curve, wallpapering all other previous/similar cards? Note:
your poker/wwstick example does not apply unless you can show how WWS
is better in EVERY conceivable instance of having either a poker or a
WWstick.

> A good example of what I have in mind is spiritus. The spiritus have
> better combat than auspex have but worse combat than animalismus have.
> The reverse is true with regarding of intercept capabilities. That way
> spiritus feels different and ANI/AUS deck have better intercept and
> worse combat than ANI/SPI as a result.

Well, yes. POT/ANI has a different feel (and worse intercept but
better combat) than ANI/AUS. So what?

> So result of some kind of card restriction would be that each subset
> would have different feel but would be balanced overall.

Assuming each subset was not any weaker or stronger than any other
given subset, then yes, we would possibly have different flavors in
each one.

We now have three choices:

1. We retroactively assign library cards to a "grouping", thus making
thousands of existing decks illegal and horribly altering the game.

2. We start grouping library cards from this point forward to a
grouping (say all existing ones are "group 1").

-Problem with 2: New group will be extremely small compared to group
1. Less cards->less variety->less power.

Solutions to problem:

-a. Print absurdly powerful cards in the beginning. Your whole
argument about power scale goes right out the window.

-b. Print an absurd amount of new cards. We're basically going to
have 2 completely different games, that can field decks against each
other or within themselves. How long would a set of this size take to
make with proper playtesting and development time? I don't want a
different game. I spend enough collecting for this one.

3. Magic: the Gathering. Raise your hand if you want to go that
route.

-Snapcase
