Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Karol Magda wrote:
>
> [snip]
>
> > How things are at this instant? Obviously not. At least, it's not completely accurate,
> > although it's also not that clear how much things have changed. As of a couple of years
> > ago, my view was accurate enough. Certainly enough to make a number of relevant
> > observations about the differences between Magic and Jyhad that you missed or
> > the you were waving your hand over.
>
> Which ones did I miss (or wawed my hand over). Restate them.

Well, the one I keep shouting at you over and over again is the Magic designers and the
Jyhad designers have different policies about unbalanced cards. The Jyhad designers tend
fix anything significantly more powerful than the norm - in fact, in my view they're so
persnickety that they often can't resist the urge to fix fairly marginal or downright non-
existant "problems". The Magic designers will not fix anything unless its causing a
very extreme problem. The number of unbalanced cards that go unchecked in their card
population is what causes many of the things that you cite as causing problems over the
long term.

Then there's the card limit issue. Magic is 4CL, Jyhad is NCL. I feel the difference
makes Jyhad designers much more sensitive to the issue of card combination interactions -
both the desirable and the undesirable ones. I have seen evidence in the design of the
Jyhad cards that Jyhad designers put some thought into this. In all the years I followed
Magic, I never once got the impression that Magic designers do anything to prevent problems
with this except (usually) avoiding the repetition of a mistake they had previously made.
Other than that, they seem to just waltz from one blunder to the next.

Then there's the number of new Magic cards that systematically get designed every year.
Two (relatively) "small" expansions and one complete new standalone. I don't know how
many cards can reasonably and reliably be designed and play-tested in a given year before
mistakes become prevalent. But I feel that Jyhad expansions, on the whole, are much better
balanced and have far fewer mistakes than Magic expansions and I have to think time spent
on each expansion has got to be one reason for it. For one thing, the print cycle makes
it impossible to do much if any testing of two adjacent expansions by playtesters in Magic.
If they would slow down the rate of expansions, quality would likely be much better but as
of the time I bought my last box of Magic cards, they showed no sign they were even
considering doing so.

Those differences will do for starters.

> > I indicated that
> > a certain class of cards existed: the class of cards that were designed and
> > printed in the past in older Magic expansions that WOULD NOT AND COULD NOT
> > be printed in the next expansion because of their very nature: they are
> > considered to be too powerful or too radical to risk printing such a card.
>

> Even without that class of cards such vast formats are impossible to
> balance (unless you restrict the card interaction in some way, and
> that's what grouping is all about, restricting card interaction so
> format become more manageable)

That statement is baseless. Of course they could balance T1.5. Just errata or
ban the unbalanced cards. That's all. Granted, there may be an unusually high
portion of cards in certain expansions (e.g. Alpha, Beta, Arabian Nights, Legends)
which would be affected. But so? The WHOLE GAME is fucked up right now because
of this. It's not like you'd have to mess with more than 10-15% of the cards in
any one expansion (maybe 20% on the outside). And the percentage of cards overall
would likely be 3% or less. That's a small price to pay in order to resolve the
problems felt by all of the older players in the game who feel their past purchases
of cards are ultimately becoming worthless.

> (about grinning demon part 21)
>
> > OK. Because it's not a 5/5 creature that has only one point of damage per turn
> > as a drawback. Grinning Demon's drawback is much worse then Juzam's.
>
> > Of course, this whole line of argument is mindless. The evaluation of which
> > creatures are or are not as good as which other creatures are clearly subjective.
> > You might make a decent argument if the two cards were near identical but they're
> > obviously not that much alike. So we're wasting our time.
>
> You forgot to take Morph mechanics in account

Sure. It's an advantage over Juzam but I'm not very impressed by it.

> We are wasting our time with this entire debate since we have zero
> control on what vtes future will bring ;)

I'm not sure what the import of that statement is. We have no control over the
future of Magic but we're not arguing about the future of Magic. We're arguing
about the future of Jyhad based on your reliance on examples from Magic's past.

> > > > (Comments elided which contained no new arguments.)
> > >
> > > It's easier to elide them and write some smart line than to answer
> > > them, don't you think ?
> >
> > No I don't think. I removed them because I *already* answered them and you never
> > responded to my answers. I'm not prepared to go mindlessly arguing in circles
> > because you don't care to address the points I made.
>
> Why do I have exactly same (reversed) feeling ? ;)

Because we likely are not understanding one another. I agree - past experience has
shown that this is often a reciprocal state of affairs.

> I restated my position so you could better reply to my position (and
> in turn I could better understand you). Sadly you passed the
> oportinity.

I passed on it because 1) you should easily be able to look for yourself at what I
said the first time you made these assertions; and 2) my experience when this happens
is that if you didn't understand my answers the first time, chances are you will not
understand them again and you will continue to restate your assertions without regard
to my answers a third and likely subsequent times in the future. Posts just get
longer and longer as neither side ever hears the other. Nothing gets resolved by such
restatements.

> > Concerning whether Weighted Walking Stick obsolesces ("wallpaperizes") Poker,
> > thus demonstrating Karol's idea that cards become systematically obsolete over

> > the course of time, Karol wrote:
> > > I stated two examples of decks where WWStick is far superior to poker.
> > > You didn't showed ANY counterexample...
> >
> > I don't have to show any counterexample. One, two, or ten examples of how one
> > card is better in a given deck than another shows nothing. To demonstrate
> > obsolescence, you must show that the card you believe is superior is the better
> > choice in *all* decks at *all* times. Or I'll settle for, "in the vast majority of
> > times" for practical purposes. You can't give only one or two examples and expect
> > anyone to accept this. To demonstrate this point, you must use inductive reasoning.
> > For instance: two weapons that cost the same but one causes more damage than the
> > other some of time and has no drawbacks that the other doesn't also have. If you
> > cannot do this, your assertion is not proved.
>
> The instance you are refering is clearly instance stricly
> inferior/superior cards (chainsaw/gas powered chainsaw). I explained
> why such thinking is stupid and give some nice examples. You failed to
> respond to that.

I failed to respond to that because it was lost in the middle of text which made
a number of various rambling and somewhat irrelevant remarks about how you feel about
the state of the game. My first recommendation is that in the future, if you have
multiple examples of something you want to cite to prove something, use the best,
simplest, most obvious one. Poker and Weighted Walking Stick simply do not demonstrate
the problem you claim they do. Either card may be preferable in a situation depending
on the details of that situation. If you want to bring up the issue of strictly one
card strictly obsolescing another, then use the Chainsaw/GP Chainsaw example in the
*first place*. That way we spend less time on side issues. (Though your reasoning on
the obsolescence of Poker is so bad, I can't resist responding to it below anyway.)

As far as Chainsaw/GP Chainsaw, this is a *mistake*. Card designers do not deliberately
print one card that is supposed to make another one obsolete but sometimes it happens
by accident (more or less). I never claimed the designers never made mistakes. In fact,
I believe I've already addressed this point: if by mistake, the designers create a new
card that's too strong, they can issue errata or ban it and thus fix it. At least,
*Jyhad* designers can. So can Magic designers - but they won't. If by mistake, the
designers print a card that's too weak, people can just ignore it and not play with it.
No major harm done.

In this case, the mistake was likely not Gas Powered Chainsaw. The mistake was likely
the first card printed, Chainsaw. It was too weak. WotC didn't even bother to reprint
it in the second edition. They printed a strictly better card in The Sabbat, and no one
has to use Chainsaw. But Chainsaw was too weak whether a better card was printed in The
Sabbat or not. So your concern about card obsolescence is still irrelevant: it's not
that a better card was printed after Chainsaw, it's that Chainsaw was too weak in the
first place. If this happens again in the future, it's fine for White Wolf to print
a better card that obsolesces a overly weak current card. This is not a problem.

> Now it's time for some inductive reasoning :)
>
> I will demonstrate that in almost every deck I want put poker in
> WWStick is better. Therefore as a result Poker is walpaperized by
> WWStick
>
> These are the decks I might want to have Poker in:
>
> 1) !Salubri
> 2) Midcap/weenie CEL close range combat
> 3) source of permanent damage for intercept combat

These might be the decks *you* want to have Poker in. But they are no
the only decks in which someone might want to use a poker. Therefore, you
haven't covered all possibilities.

I don't think you understand the concept of "inductive reasoning".
You can't just wave your hand and severely limit the environment in
which Poker is used. You have to _prove_ WWS is always better.

> case 1) and 2) was explained
> case 3) is easy to explain too since I will not use poker more than
> three times in such deck and it saves me an action to equip

I don't agree with these, either. But it doesn't matter. The whole
proof is already wrong.

> How can disciplinless reusable version of Torn Signpost not
> wallpaperize poker ?

Because you must use a difference copy of Torn Signpost each combat.
Once you equip with Poker, it normally stays in place - excepting the
usual means of removing it and its own special means. It doesn't have
to be redrawn every combat. Both cards have their virtues and
drawbacks - and even be used together.

> [snipped many things]
>
> > > Again, you didn't show anything. It's irrelevant whether I have
> > > precognition or spirit's touch superior effect most of the time. What
> > > is relevant is to reduce chance of clumping my hand with multiply
> > > copies of same intercept card.
> >
> > *Most* of the time. BUT NOT *ALL* THE TIME. You are assuming the designers
> > intend that the number of intercept cards available to use at inferior is supposed
> > to be limited. GET IT THROUGH YOUR HEAD: THAT'S *YOUR* ASSUMPTION! IT'S *NOT*
> > MY ASSUMPTION!!! I showed that there could be another reason that multiple Auspex
> > intercept cards exist: so they can do something else at superior. Since I don't
> > assume what you assume, and because there's no reason anyone *ELSE* should assume
> > what you assume, your theories about how this relates to grouping library cards
> > are questionable.
> > ...
>
> Screaming is unnecessary.

Sorry, I get frustrated. I feel your reasoning is very bad and this is leading
to many errors in your conclusions. In this case, you point out accurate facts
but the conclusion you draw from them is obviously (to me) unfounded. I've
challenged it several times, yet you ignore or misunderstand the challenge and
act as if your conclusion about the facts is reasonable. I get tired of that.

> When in trouble or in doubt run in circles scream and shout.

I'll try to keep that in mind, in the future.

> I consider that your arguments failed you here. If you want to prove
> me otherwise you must restate your position in more polite version.

Do what you want. The point is, there is no issue here. You simply refuse to
accept that unlimited numbers of Auspex intercept cards that give +1 intercept
at inferior and do something unique at superior is not likely to be considered
a problem by most reasonable people. I can't help that. It is not a good
reason to group library cards.



Well, make the case if you can. I think we've chewed on this long enough to resolve
that: 1) You believe this could be a problem in some environments; and 2) I believe this
might now be a problem in some other environments; and 3) we don't seem to be able to
convince one another that it is either always or never a problem because it really depends
on what the power curve of the cards look like and that power curve likely varies from
one environment to the next.

You are also ignoring the point that how often a solution works is not the only criteria
for deciding which solution is superior. If you're having problems with mice, you can set
up mouse traps and get a cat. Or you can blow up your house, have the rubbish hauled away,
and build a new house. I'll bet the second solution eliminates the problem more often
than the first. Reasons why it might not be the *best* solution for the problem are left
as an exercise for the student.

> Very few cards are bad on their own, strength of fifth tradition would
> be less of a issue if minion tap would not exists. Again card
> interaction is what is problematic.

It depends on what you mean. Card strength requires context, of course. But when the
context are other unquestioned, backbone-of-the-game cards, this is an absurd, pedantic
argument. Return to Innocence caused a problem because it made huge, game-winning bleeds
possible - but only in combination with either lots of stealth or something like Day
Operation that made the bleed unblockable. (Bounce notwithstanding, as it was decided
that failure to play bounce should not cost someone a game by itself.) So one could ask,
"Is Return to Innocence the problem or are all the stealth and unblockability cards the
problem?" The answer is very obvious if you're being reasonable.

Given that point, I strongly disagree with you. Most cards that are bad are identifiable
as being problem cards _themselves_ - not simply in combination with other cards. Fifth
Tradition is seen as the problem card because it fills any sized vampire from zero to
capacity regardless of whether you can or cannot Minion Tap it afterward. Minion Tap,
at the same time, is considered a staple or a foundation of the game. It cannot be
removed or modified without making major modifications to many aspects of the game. So,
yes - Fifth Tradition is the issue. Period.

Strangely enough - and likely not coincidentally - I've had this exact same argument with
other people: all Magic players. This way of seeing card balance in a CCG seems to me to
be an obfuscation used to justify not solving real problems in Magic. This habit of
excusing bad cards for being bad "only because they require other cards to function" is
just an excuse for ducking the problem and not doing anything. So instead of fixing
cards, you wind up rotating whole expansions out of an environment and thus causing all
the problems Magic currently has. Stupid, stupid, stupid!

> > In this case, I assert these counterexamples don't even prove *THAT*: 1) Magic examples,
> > as I've stated many times don't apply. The DCI doesn't ban all abusive cards anyway
> > so who cares what happens in Magic? Black Vise was abusive, Land Tax was abusive, and
> > Necropotence was abusive. In this case, the problem is that the DIC just didn't ban
> > enough cards to get near the point of fixing the problem. Doesn't mean the problem
> > couldn't be fixed. It just means the DCI wasn't willing to do what truly needed to be
> > done. 2) I don't agree that recent CE erratas of power cards were necessary, anyway.
> > That the V:tES designers seem a bit over finicky about the slightly more powerful cards
> > says nothing about the generally principle that's in dispute. And even if they were
> > necessary, who said there were any more abusive cards?
>
> You stated many things many times , you didn't proved many things though.

They're opinions, I agree. I am giving my opinions about why Magic is the way it is
as alternative to _your_ opinions about the same issues - which are not proved, either.
No one person can prove anything about these things unless he is given the power to
try. Put me in charge of the DCI and I'll prove some things to you.

> Examples of the cards which might be changed in future:
>
> Dreams of Sphinx, Powerbase Montreal, Conditioning, Govern the
> Unaligned, PtO
>
> The case could be made:
>
> 1) some of them are no brainers

Sorry, I have to laugh at this one. Dreams of the Sphinx and Powerbase: Montreal are
on my list of being two of the more overrated cards in the game. They do have specific
uses. But people use them a lot more often than can possibly be explained. Why are
they so popular? Who knows?

The other two, Conditions and Govern the Unaligned are classic staple cards. They
were in the original Jyhad edition, have been reprinted many times, and are common
cards. All signs that a card should be considered a staple, not overpowered.

> 2) they disable more archetypes than they enable

Certainly Dreams of the Sphinx and Powerbase: Montreal do no such thing.

It's fairly conjectural about the other two. As I said, they're part of the whole
foundation of the game. It's possible you could get rid of them and redesign the
game into something richer and more interesting. But they've been in the game since
day one so it's very tricky to say what the game would look like without them. I
don't see any reason to bother.

> 3) they turn the game to a fight over a control of this resource

Only Powerbase: Montreal does that. And it was designed to do that. And I don't
see why that's a bad thing.

> > > Look. T1.5 have like 10 000 of cards. Most of the cards can interact
> > > with themselves one way or another. Just compute the number of
> > > two/three/four cards combos. (waiting for him to do so....) See, big
> > > number isn't it ? Well and any of this combo can be really abusive.
> > > How can you prevent it from happening ?
>
> > You stay alert to it as you design the cards. Part of the problem is that
> > Magic designers are careless and put out expansions far too quickly to properly
> > balance cards. And when they do make mistakes, they leave them in the game
> > as is instead of fixing them. So *of course* you get problems like this.
>
> which is not true for extended,t2,block constructed

Sure. Because of the limited number of cards. Basically, they ban whole expansions
to solve problems instead of specific individual cards. If you ever need surgery,
I hope your doctor does not think like this. Otherwise, you will see him walk into
the operating room with an ax instead of a scalpel. (All the worse if what you need
is brain surgery.)

(The rest snipped because I believe we're down to differences in judgment. Not
disputes that are likely to be resolvable.)

Fred

On Thu, 14 Nov 2002, Derek Ray wrote:

> Jaroslav Pascek would much rather have a Poker.

I don't think Poker is in any way wall-papered by WWS. However, I'm not
sure about your specific example. I'm assuming if you're doing Pokers and
Pascek that you're also playing with DW, since Pascek is huge (meaning you
want to maximize his action-efficiency) and doesn't have access to much in
the way of stealth. If you grant that, then the WWS is a stand-alone
card, which is clearly better than a two card combo. With one combat
card, Pascek is hitting for four, and then four again with
Pursuit. That's eight damage out of one combat card. If he's foiled by
S:CE, no counters go on the card and it's ready to be used again. WWS is
transient, so Poker gets points for sticking around, but eight damage out
of one card is a pretty good return, and much more reliable than waiting
for the combo.

David Cherryholmes
Prince of Durham, NC

Of course. The standard rule still applies; any CEL minion taking an action
to equip with a weapon is an action that is worth losing a minion "now" to
block, because it means you won't lose lots of minions "later".

> card, which is clearly better than a two card combo. With one combat
> card, Pascek is hitting for four, and then four again with
> Pursuit. That's eight damage out of one combat card. If he's foiled by

A two-card combo is not significantly more difficult to get in hand than a
one-card combo, though -- we do it all the time over the course of the
game, since very few single cards can provide an effect AND all appropriate
modifiers (stealth being a biggie). Especially so for combat decks.

Sure, you can be unlucky and not happen to get both CW and the weapon in
hand relatively early on, but that's more of a deckbuilding issue.

> S:CE, no counters go on the card and it's ready to be used again. WWS is
> transient, so Poker gets points for sticking around, but eight damage out
> of one card is a pretty good return, and much more reliable than waiting
> for the combo.

And now the potential problems: a minion may have only one Weighted Walking
Stick. With Jaroslav breaking the damn things every other time he swings
one (think The Hulk hitting people with a pool cue), you have to put a LOT
of WWS in the deck in order to keep him properly equipped... risking a
nasty case of hand jam if you don't constantly get into combat. Yes, you
can hand one off to each of your other minions as well, but that requires
that THOSE minions get into combat, and they may not be as-well equipped to
deal with the situation as Jaroslav (the deck idea here being Jaroslav as
the enforcer/defender, with a number of PRE weenies to hand out bleeds).

All things considered, I'd ACTUALLY rather just pay 1 pool and give him a
Bastard Sword. Permanent, doesn't break to Fortitude or Potence, and the
pool cost is really negligible in the end, since the long-term efficiency
is so good.

-- Derek

> is valid example, so be it. Nobody (so far) explained why it is not
> better to use WWS over Poker. (I explained my position, though)

See Derek's post for counterexamples. Thus it has not been shown that
WWS is better than Poker (and there *are* non-cornercase examples of
Poker being better than WWS).

> > 1. We retroactively assign library cards to a "grouping", thus making
> > thousands of existing decks illegal and horribly altering the game.
>
> Do you really feel that there are thousands decks avaiable ?

Yes, I do. I haven't counted, but I'd venture to guess there's that
there's several hundred in Lasombra Jeff's archives alone.

> That was not case when grouping of vampire cards was introduced. :)

I think you're severely underestimating the number of decks out there.
Just go to http://www.thelasombra.com/WhosWho/ . About 42 people and
there's about 810 decks between them.

> > 2. We start grouping library cards from this point forward to a
> > grouping (say all existing ones are "group 1").
>

> No, I would not go with way two (as proposed)

Good.

> > 3. Magic: the Gathering. Raise your hand if you want to go that
> > route.
>
> Depends ;) I want to play with all of my cards yet I want to see
> metagame changes too. (it might be possible that these two
> requirements are mutually exclusive)

In M:tG they are mutually exclusive. Groups rotate out, and are no
longer legal for the "standard" tournament type. You can play with
all the cards you want in Type 1 or 1.5, but good luck finding a
tournament for them.

> 4) group library cards in similar way it was done with vampire cards.

The problem with that is that many library cards were reprinted
between many sets, while vampires were not (only between Jyhad/Vtes
and Sab/SW). CE is basically a collected reprint of previous sets.
So you'd have a grouping that wouldn't really mean anything for some
cards, and yet limit others. Indeed, some of the cards that wouldn't
be limited are the ones you were posting as examples of "powercards
that have risen to the top with the CE changes" (i.e. Govern the
Unaligned and Conditioning).

> 5) never openly group cards. Instead introduce say "dark ages"
> "ancient ages" "victorian ages" versions of current disciplines with
> possible crossover to existing ones if flavour allows (bloodlines
> style)

How is this much different from #2 above? You're putting all the
current stuff in the "modern age" and the next "group" of library
cards would be "dark ages".

> 6)print new cards to existing disciplines without abovementioned
> siliness
> (I understand that that is an option too :) )

Indeed. It seems to be the current policy, and it seems to be
working.

-Snapcase

*GROANNNNNNNNNNN*!!! You've missed the point AGAIN!!! The point has
nothing to do with whether the design teams choose to ban vs. errata.
Either will suffice. Both fix problems with overpowered cards.
It's the quality of cards *THAT* the designers of either game choose to
ban or errata that's the critical difference. WotC leaves overpowered
cards in place. WW doesn't. The difference exactly explains why things
come to a head when the card population gets to thousands of cards.

> (Fred: 4CL vs NCL)
>
> 4CL in magic (almost) directly translate to 6CL in Jyhad. It was
> demonstrated (by Legbiter IIRC) that one can build 6CL deck and be
> competitive in NCL enviroment.

I'm not sure what this has to do with the metagame, however. Nor do
I even agree that it's true. I don't know what Legbiter may have shown,
but it's clear that XCL environments are necessarily different than
playing under NCL. Thus, certain decks that are viable under a give XCL
environment may very well not be viable under NCL. Some decks may but
others are not.

Anyway, it's not relevant. How decks translate from one environment to
another has nothing to do with designing cards under either environment
and demonstrates a complete misunderstanding of the point I was trying
to make.

> Most of the NCL decks can be translated to 6CL enviroment prety nicely too.

Really? I'd like to see how a Shadow Twin deck works under 6 CL.

> Not that big difference.

Well, sorry I think it is.

> (Fred: Speed of how new magic product is prepared)
>
> WotC has lot of resources so that they (can) have wast army of
> testers.

And how does this address the problem of testing adjacent expansions?
Before you suggest it, I will tell you WotC Netreps have said straight out that
no playtest groups are ever given multiple expansions to test simultaneously.
It's a problem that cannot be solved by pure numbers. It requires more time
between expansions.

> Also less time is needed to discover potentially abusive
> combos than in Vamipre given the fact that average Magic game last
> what? 15 minutes and average V:TES game last 1 hour and 30 minutes
> (although more testing data is gathered from average V:TES game than
> from average Magic game)
>
> When all taken into consideration, not that big difference.

Well, sorry, I think it is. This one in particular is based on anecdotal
evidence so we're not likely to find a way to resolve it. But it's really
not central to my argument so it doesn't matter.

> > Those differences will do for starters.
>
> Those differencies are quite irrelevant (or not that different)

If you don't think so, then you're going to assume the experiences of two unlike
products will be the same over time. I can't help that. I've played Magic for
years and I've been a critic of these things for years. (Well, not the 4CL thing.
The 4CL thing in Magic is necessary - but the difference it causes between the
two games is certainly real enough whether you agree with Magic's 4CL or not.)
I've played Jyhad for years and these things are not a problem in Jyhad. So now
you want me to believe that Jyhad needs grouping of library cards to solve
problems that are not *in* Jyhad at all? Forget it. You're trying to shoehorn
an unnecessary solution that isn't even necessary for Magic into Jyhad's world
for no good reason.

Below, I've snipped a lot of content based on these differences. There isn't
much point to posting whole, long arguments that just snipe back and forth
without much further to say. I've lodged my objections to the concept of using
Magic as an "older brother" example of what will happen to Jyhad in the future.
You reject my objections but don't give satisfactory reasons why they're incorrect
or irrelevant. So we're stuck.

> My original remark was that although there are few strictly superior
> cards in V:TES (like GPChainsaw vs Chainsaw example) still there are
> cards which are used almost always compared to their alternative (I
> gave examples of GtU/ Scounting Mission, Deflection/Redirection,
> Telepatic Misdirection/My Enemies Enemy and WWStick/Poker). (and how
> therefore the weaker alternative are wallpaperized kind of (or
> cornercased or whatever)
>
> To that you still do not responded.

That statement is also baseless. I've responded to all these things.
In essence:

1) Chainsaw was a mistake and the fact that WotC later printing a
useful card that obsolesces Chainsaw does not demonstrate any problem.

2) Weighted Walking Stick does not obsolesce Poker period - a point that
others besides me have disputed and which I notice no one else besides
you has yet attempted to defend.

(By the way, tell that to the guy who showed up with a bunch of Pokers
in his deck at our Storyline tournament last Sunday. No, he did *not*
care to replace them with Weighted Walking Sticks in spite of your
opinion, thank you very much...)

3) The others are not examples of obsolescence, either. All have uses
in different situations. (And I have seem prolific use of Scouting
Mission, Redirection, and My Enemy's Enemy in the decks of very
respectable players at Gencon and elsewhere. In fact, My Enemy's Enemy
is considered a premium card! Certain people would be very surprised
at your opinion of it.)

> > > Now it's time for some inductive reasoning :)

...

> > I don't think you understand the concept of "inductive reasoning".
> > You can't just wave your hand and severely limit the environment in
> > which Poker is used. You have to _prove_ WWS is always better.
>
> I can (always) restrict proof to cover only relevant cases (case: Deck
> I want not to put poker in is irrelevant)

Only if you *prove* they're not relevant - which you didn't bother to
do. And I believe you cannot do.

> > > How can disciplinless reusable version of Torn Signpost not
> > > wallpaperize poker ?
>
> > Because you must use a difference copy of Torn Signpost each combat.
>

> Uhm, there is word: Reusable in my statement above.

Sorry, I missed the significance of that. But the answer is the same.
WWS is only somewhat reusable - it breaks after 1-3 uses. Poker only
breaks against fortitude. So it cannot obsolesce Poker.

> > The point is, there is no issue here. You simply refuse to accept that
> > unlimited numbers of Auspex intercept cards that give +1 intercept at
> > inferior and do something unique at superior is not likely to be considered
> > a problem by most reasonable people. I can't help that. It is not a good
> > reason to group library cards.
>
> Most reasonoble people , eh ? I am completely reasonable here. In fact
> since I have great success with intercept decks (like winning
> tournaments (even big ones) ) with them (where most people claim that
> intercept can't win) I don't really care what reasonable people tell
> (unless they provide some empirical data I can provide on that topic)
>
> If you can provide them good, we can discuss. If not get lost.

I'm not sure what any of this has to do with grouping library cards. So
you've won some games with intercept, so what? What has this to do with
the potential problem of too many Auspex intercept cards which do the
same thing (grant +1 intercept) at inferior but do something different at
superior? Sounds to me like evidence that most other people don't believe
there's _enough_ different intercept cards. Be that as it may, who cares?

> [snip]
[snip, indeed]

> > You are also ignoring the point that how often a solution works is not the only criteria
> > for deciding which solution is superior. If you're having problems with mice, you can set
> > up mouse traps and get a cat. Or you can blow up your house, have the rubbish hauled away,
> > and build a new house. I'll bet the second solution eliminates the problem more often
> > than the first.
>

> This example is quite wrong (in the context of this discussion since
> the difference between solutions are more subtle).

It demonstrates my point: simple effectiveness in solving a problem is not
the only criteria. You also need to make sure that the side-effects caused
by your solution aren't worse than the original problem.

> > > Very few cards are bad on their own, strength of fifth tradition would
> > > be less of a issue if minion tap would not exists. Again card
> > > interaction is what is problematic.
>
> > It depends on what you mean. Card strength requires context, of course. But when the
> > context are other unquestioned, backbone-of-the-game cards, this is an absurd, pedantic
> > argument. Return to Innocence caused a problem because it made huge, game-winning bleeds
> > possible - but only in combination with either lots of stealth or something like Day
> > Operation that made the bleed unblockable. (Bounce notwithstanding, as it was decided
> > that failure to play bounce should not cost someone a game by itself.) So one could ask,
> > "Is Return to Innocence the problem or are all the stealth and unblockability cards the
> > problem?" The answer is very obvious if you're being reasonable.
>
> Irrelevant. My comment was very few cards are bad on their own.

No cards are "bad on their own" by that definition of "bad". But it's a useless
definition. You can not discern bad from good without a context so showing that
cards are not bad outside of the context in which they are used essentially says
nothing at all.

> > Given that point, I strongly disagree with you. Most cards that are bad are identifiable
> > as being problem cards _themselves_ - not simply in combination with other cards. Fifth
> > Tradition is seen as the problem card because it fills any sized vampire from zero to
> > capacity regardless of whether you can or cannot Minion Tap it afterward. Minion Tap,

> > yes - Fifth Tradition is the issue. Period.
>

> less of a issue if Minion Tap didn't existed.

I suppose. But Minion Tap is a staple card so it doesn't matter. Minion Tap exists, must
exist, and will continue to exist in the future. So it's a moot point.

> [snip]
[snip, indeed]

> Again not listening. Again providing bad example. Again mildly insulting at it.

...and that's the problem. You're prepared to proposed this extreme solution based on your
insistence on comparing Jyhad to a completely different game has been designed, expanded, and
maintained using demonstrably inferior policies and you get "mildly insulted" when someone
inconveniently points these things out to you. These points will exist whether you consider
them "good examples" or not. Either way, it doesn't matter.
